# How Do You Cross the Flood?

*SN 1.1, the Oghataraṇa Sutta — set 2, The Basic Diagnosis and the Path*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 1 min · 170 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

A deity asks one direct question: how did the Buddha cross a flood? His answer
sounds impossible. Standing still makes him sink, while struggling makes him
get swept away. He crosses by doing neither.

The text does not define the flood here. The image is enough to begin with:
it is something powerful that can overwhelm you and carry you along. The
answer also does not mean "make no effort." Standing still and struggling are
both shown to fail. The short exchange asks whether there is a way of moving
that is neither passive collapse nor frantic forcing.

Read the dialogue once before opening the word explanations. Its unresolved
tension is the teaching, not a puzzle the introduction should solve for you.

## Translation

### A Question in the Night

So I have heard.

At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove,
Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.

Late one night, a radiant deity lit up the whole of Jeta's Grove. The deity
approached the Buddha, bowed, stood to one side, and asked:

"My friend, how did you cross over the flood?"

"Friend, I crossed over the flood without standing still and without
struggling."

"But my friend, how did you cross over the flood without standing still or
struggling?"

"When I stood still, I sank.

When I struggled, I was swept away.

That is how I crossed over the flood without standing still or struggling."

### The Deity's Verse

"After such a long time, at last I see
a brahmin who has reached complete quenching.
Without standing still and without struggling,
they have crossed over the world's entanglement."

The Teacher agreed with what the deity had said.

Thinking, "The Teacher agrees with me," the deity bowed to the Buddha,
circled him clockwise, and vanished right there.

<dd>Originally a member of ancient India&#x27;s hereditary priestly class. These texts sometimes reuse the title for an ideal practitioner who has completed the path, so context determines whether caste or conduct is meant.</dd>

<dd>The complete going out of greed, aversion, and delusion. In AN 3.69 and SN 1.1 it describes what is reached while alive, not death.</dd>

<dd>Having completed the crossing rather than merely moving toward the other side. This preserves the river image used for completion of the path.</dd>

<dd>A divine being in the ancient Indian cosmology. In SN 1.1 the deity is a nighttime visitor who asks the Buddha a question, not a creator god.</dd>
<dt><dfn>flood</dfn></dt>
<dd>A force that overwhelms and carries a person along unless it is crossed. SN 1.1 leaves the image open rather than defining it as one specific mental state.</dd>

<dd>An extinguishing image for dissatisfaction and its causes going out. Different Pali words use this image on different pages, so the exact scope comes from the sentence.</dd>

*[brahmin]: Originally a member of ancient India's hereditary priestly class. These texts sometimes reuse the title for an ideal practitioner who has completed the path, so context determines whether caste or conduct is meant.
*[complete quenching]: The complete going out of greed, aversion, and delusion. In AN 3.69 and SN 1.1 it describes what is reached while alive, not death.
*[crossed over]: Having completed the crossing rather than merely moving toward the other side. This preserves the river image used for completion of the path.
*[deity]: A divine being in the ancient Indian cosmology. In SN 1.1 the deity is a nighttime visitor who asks the Buddha a question, not a creator god.
*[flood]: A force that overwhelms and carries a person along unless it is crossed. SN 1.1 leaves the image open rather than defining it as one specific mental state.
*[quenching]: An extinguishing image for dissatisfaction and its causes going out. Different Pali words use this image on different pages, so the exact scope comes from the sentence.
*[world]: A common word in these texts that shifts meaning by context -- sometimes the physical cosmos beings are reborn into, sometimes (as in MN 63) a specific philosophical question about whether existence as a whole is eternal or finite. Each sutta's own framing makes clear which sense is meant.
*[world's entanglement]: The sticky web of wanting and taking things personally that keeps a person caught in the experienced world.
